seoTitle: Hot Swollen Joint: Septic Arthritis vs Gout, Step by Step
metaDescription: The hot swollen joint for EM, IM and peds rotations: when to tap, synovial fluid cutoffs, antibiotics by Gram stain, gout, pseudogout, the limping child.
h1: The hot swollen joint: septic arthritis, gout and the workup, fork by fork
dek: For the student on an EM, IM or peds rotation with a hot, swollen joint and a resident about to ask what is next: the three questions before the needle, what the fluid means, antibiotics by Gram stain, gout and pseudogout flares, the limping child, and what you will be pimped on.

shortAnswer.text: Septic? A joint replacement? A bleeding disorder or an anticoagulant? Sepsis means antibiotics within the hour, a prosthesis goes to orthopedics, and hemophilia gets factor before any tap.
Stable native joint: arthrocentesis for culture, Gram stain, crystals and a white cell count with differential, plus two sets of blood cultures. An anticoagulant is not a bar to the tap.

shortAnswer.lead: Read the count, not just the crystals.
shortAnswer.text: A WBC over 50,000 with 90% neutrophils suggests a bacterial joint; under 50,000 does not rule infection out, and crystals do not rule out a septic joint alongside them.

Gram-positive cocci: IV vancomycin. Gram-negative rods: vancomycin plus ceftriaxone, or plus ceftazidime 2 g IV every 12 hours with injection drug use. Stain negative but septic: vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin.

shortAnswer.lead: A septic native joint gets drained.
shortAnswer.text: Arthrotomy, arthroscopy or daily needle aspiration, chosen by orthopedics; nongonococcal: about 2 weeks IV, then oral, 3 to 4 weeks in all (4 to 6 with Pseudomonas).
An NSAID, colchicine 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg an hour later, or prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day or more for 5 to 10 days. Established allopurinol keeps going, and the culture is still followed.

shortAnswer.lead: Gonococcal arthritis is not a single shot.
shortAnswer.text: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV or IM every 24 hours, plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days unless chlamydia is excluded, with specimens from every exposed site.

shortAnswer.lead: The limping child: ultrasound, labs, Kocher.
shortAnswer.text: An effusion with risk features gets an ultrasound-guided aspirate, and a septic aspirate gets urgent irrigation and debridement. Low risk: rest, an NSAID and observation when unsure.

sections.heading: What do you do first for a hot swollen joint?
sections.intro: Consider septic arthritis in every hot, swollen joint, and ask three questions before the needle: sepsis, a joint replacement, and a bleeding disorder or anticoagulant.

sections.heading: What do the synovial fluid results mean?
sections.intro: The Gram stain picks the antibiotic, the count and the fever decide whether a negative stain is still treated, and crystals with a count under 50,000, or blood, send the joint down their own branch. The hip aspirate, the Kocher criteria and the urate history fork the same way.

sections.heading: Prosthetic joint, gonococcus or a septic hip: what changes the workup?
sections.intro: A joint replacement is aspirated by orthopedics; suspected disseminated gonococcal infection needs specimens from every exposed site; a child's hip with risk features is aspirated under ultrasound; inflammatory fluid without crystals or organisms gets Lyme serology after tick exposure and trigger testing.

sections.heading: What antibiotics for septic arthritis, and how is gout treated?
sections.intro: Empiric cover by the Gram stain with antistaphylococcal cover in every septic joint and drainage by orthopedics; gout, pseudogout, gonococcal and Lyme arthritis each have their own regimen.

sections.heading: Which labs, and how do you tap a hot joint?
sections.intro: Adult native joint: synovial fluid for culture, Gram stain, crystals and cell count, two sets of blood cultures, CBC, ESR and CRP. Limping child: hip ultrasound and x-ray with WBC, ESR and CRP.

sections.heading: Transient synovitis or a first gout flare: who goes home?
sections.intro: Transient synovitis is supportive care, with observation when the diagnosis is unclear; after a first uncomplicated gout flare ACR 2020 conditionally advises against starting urate-lowering therapy, and the urate is rechecked once it settles.

sections.heading: Where does each hot joint end up?
sections.intro: Native septic joints to drainage and 3 to 4 weeks of antibiotics (a child's septic hip about 10 to 14 days when uncomplicated; a joint replacement usually surgery and 6 weeks or more IV), crystal flares to treatment with the culture still followed, and the joints this pathway does not cover to their next workup.

checklist.heading: Before and after the tap: the hot joint checklist

items.text: Sepsis screen first: septic and unstable means antibiotics within 1 hour, with cultures first only if that adds under 45 minutes.
Joint replacement: orthopedics aspirates, and no antibiotic before the cultures unless septic.
Hemophilia: factor VIII before any imaging or needle.
Synovial fluid: white cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals.
Two sets of blood cultures; CBC, ESR and CRP.
Crystals found: follow the culture anyway.
Sexually active with tenosynovitis or skin lesions: NAAT or culture of every exposed site, plus HIV and syphilis tests.

rounds.present: Lead with the joint and the three screening questions, then the fluid and the plan. For example: 61-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis and a corticosteroid injection into the left knee 10 days ago, now 2 days of a hot, swollen left knee and unable to bear weight; temperature 38.6 C (101.5 F), HR 102, BP 138/82, stable, native joint, no joint replacement or bleeding disorder. Aspirate: turbid fluid, WBC 86,000 with 92% neutrophils, gram-positive cocci in clusters, no crystals; two sets of blood cultures sent. Plan: IV vancomycin dosed to renal function and levels, narrowed on the culture; orthopedics to drain the joint by arthroscopy, arthrotomy or daily needle aspiration; about 2 weeks IV then oral, 3 to 4 weeks in all; re-aspirate if no better in 5 to 6 days.

pimp.q: Why does the serum urate not settle gout in the ED?
pimp.a: It can be under 6 mg/dL during a flare. NICE repeats it at least 2 weeks after the flare settles.

pimp.q: Urate crystals and a WBC of 88,000. Is it gout?
pimp.a: Not safely: crystals do not rule out a septic joint alongside them. A septic-range count with a negative stain is treated with vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin while the culture runs.
Fever over 101.3 F (38.5 C), refusal to bear weight, ESR over 40 mm/h and WBC over 12,000/uL. The risk of a septic hip is 3% with one, 40% with two, 93% with three and 99% with all four.

pimp.q: Gram-negative rods in someone who injects drugs. Why ceftazidime over ceftriaxone?
pimp.a: Ceftazidime's label lists Pseudomonas aeruginosa among its bone and joint pathogens; ceftriaxone's bone and joint indication does not. StatPearls links joint infection in injection drug use to Serratia and Pseudomonas.

pimp.q: Why not a single 500 mg dose of ceftriaxone for gonococcal arthritis?
pimp.a: That is the regimen for uncomplicated cervical, urethral or rectal infection. Disseminated infection gets 1 g IV or IM every 24 hours, with doxycycline unless chlamydia is excluded.

pimp.q: Gout flare on allopurinol. Stop it?
pimp.a: No. Established urate-lowering therapy continues without interruption during a flare, and the dose is titrated by monthly urate levels toward under 6 mg/dL once it settles.

traps.text: Antibiotics before the tap in a stable patient. They wait until synovial fluid has been taken, then start promptly.
Calling it gout because crystals are seen. Crystals do not rule out a septic joint; the culture is followed.
Calling it not septic because the synovial WBC is under 50,000. That does not rule infection out.
Stopping allopurinol during a flare. Established urate-lowering therapy continues.
Colchicine 0.6 mg every hour until the pain eases. Low dose: 1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg an hour later.
Tapping a hemophilic knee before factor. Factor VIII first; any tap only under factor cover.
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once for gonococcal arthritis. That is the uncomplicated regimen, not the disseminated one.
Antibiotics alone for a septic hip in a child. It is an orthopedic emergency: urgent irrigation and debridement.

faq.q: What synovial fluid WBC count means septic arthritis?
faq.a: A WBC over 50,000 with 90% neutrophils suggests a bacterial source, but a count under 50,000 does not rule infection out, and crystals do not rule out a septic joint alongside them. A joint replacement uses far lower cutoffs: over 1,700 cells/uL supports a knee infection and over 4,200 a hip, with neutrophils over 80% typical; another StatPearls chapter gives 1,100 with 64%.

faq.q: What antibiotics are used for septic arthritis?
faq.a: Every septic joint gets antistaphylococcal cover, usually IV vancomycin when MRSA is possible. Gram-negative rods add ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g IV daily, or ceftazidime 2 g IV every 12 hours with injection drug use. A negative Gram stain with a septic picture gets vancomycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin. Drainage is part of treatment; nongonococcal joints get about 2 weeks IV, 3 to 4 weeks in all. Gonococcal arthritis has its own regimen.

faq.q: How do you treat an acute gout flare?
faq.a: An NSAID at full anti-inflammatory dose, low-dose colchicine (1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg an hour later, maximum 1.8 mg over 1 hour), or prednisone at least 0.5 mg/kg/day for 5 to 10 days, chosen by comorbidity and past response. IL-1 inhibitors wait until these fail or cannot be used. Established allopurinol continues, and the culture is still followed.

faq.q: When do you start allopurinol after a gout flare?
faq.a: When indicated: tophi, 2 or more flares a year, CKD stage 3 or more, or a first flare with a urate over 9 mg/dL or stones. After a first uncomplicated flare ACR 2020 conditionally advises against it. ACR conditionally favors starting during the flare, NICE 2 to 4 weeks after it settles. Start at 100 mg a day or less with colchicine prophylaxis, titrated to a urate under 6 mg/dL.

faq.q: How do you tell transient synovitis from a septic hip?
faq.a: Hip ultrasound and x-ray with WBC, ESR and CRP, then the Kocher criteria: fever over 101.3 F (38.5 C), refusal to bear weight, ESR over 40 mm/h, WBC over 12,000/uL. An effusion with risk features is aspirated under ultrasound; a synovial WBC over 50,000, a positive Gram stain or glucose under 40 mg/dL means a septic hip and urgent drainage.

After two-tier serology, an EIA then an immunoblot or a second FDA-cleared EIA: oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily or 200 mg once daily for 28 days, with amoxicillin as the alternative. A partial response gets a second oral course; minimal or no response gets IV ceftriaxone for 2 to 4 weeks. Synovial PCR is for a diagnosis still in doubt.
